questions.topic: Staffing ratio when a qualified worker changes assignments
questions.trigger: One pharmacist is working with one certified technician, two ordinary technicians and one licensed intern. The intern is reassigned exclusively to inventory duties, without assisting in preparing or filling prescriptions. A trainee is then assigned to the filling team. No vaccination service or waiver applies. Which adjustment would make the resulting filling team compliant? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Restore the required qualified-person mix for four filling support personnel, or reduce the filling team to three including the certified technician.
questions.critical_exception: Licensed personnel exclusively performing non-filling inventory duties are not counted under the policy; the replacement trainee is counted.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the fourth worker assisting filling is a second certified technician or an intern, the 1:4 credential mix can be met.
questions.stem: One pharmacist is working with one certified technician, two ordinary technicians and one licensed intern. The intern is reassigned exclusively to inventory duties, without assisting in preparing or filling prescriptions. A trainee is then assigned to the filling team. No vaccination service or waiver applies. Which adjustment would make the resulting filling team compliant? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Continue with all four filling workers; the intern still counts as a qualified worker despite the reassignment.
choices.why: Incorrect. The intern is not participating in filling, and the four-person filling team has only one qualified member of the required categories.

choices.text: Assign one ordinary technician to inventory only, leaving three filling support personnel including the certified technician.
choices.why: Correct. The remaining three meet the 1:3 credential condition.

choices.text: Replace the trainee assigned to filling with another certified technician.
choices.why: Correct. Two certified technicians support the 1:4 arrangement.

choices.text: Count a cashier as the second qualified filling worker because the cashier is trained at the register.
choices.why: Incorrect. The cashier is not a licensed intern or certified technician.

choices.text: Leave the four workers filling and ask the pharmacist to check more prescriptions per hour.
choices.why: Incorrect. More checks do not fix the required personnel mix.

questions.topic: Schedule II non-abuse-deterrent hydrocodone-only ER
questions.trigger: An otherwise valid prescription requires handling a hydrocodone-only extended-release product that is not abuse-deterrent. Which support person may handle the product under direct supervision of a registered pharmacist?
questions.legal_decision: Assign the task to a licensed pharmacy intern under direct pharmacist supervision; technician certification is not an exception.
questions.critical_exception: Assume the product falls exactly within the special hydrocodone-only ER restriction; the activity is handling, not transport of a filled and verified package.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the product is ordinary Schedule II stock not subject to the special restriction, a properly authorized certified technician may assist with handling under the general rule.
questions.stem: An otherwise valid prescription requires handling a hydrocodone-only extended-release product that is not abuse-deterrent. Which support person may handle the product under direct supervision of a registered pharmacist?

choices.text: A pharmacy technician trainee who has completed internal controlled-stock training.
choices.why: Incorrect. Training does not remove the express product-specific restriction.

choices.text: A state-licensed noncertified technician approved by the manager of record.
choices.why: Incorrect. Ordinary technician approval does not authorize this special handling task.

choices.text: A licensed certified technician with a written controlled-substance policy.
choices.why: Incorrect. Even certified technicians are excluded from handling this formulation.

choices.text: A licensed pharmacy intern directly supervised by the registered pharmacist.
choices.why: Correct. The regulation expressly allows directly supervised interns to handle this formulation.

choices.text: An experienced technician whose national certification recently expired.
choices.why: Incorrect. Neither an ordinary nor certified technician may perform this specific handling.

critical_error_options.reason: Assigns a expressly prohibited product-handling duty to a technician.

questions.topic: MOR responsibility after resignation
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy's manager of record resigns on Monday. The owner appoints a qualified replacement and tells the departing pharmacist that all required reporting is the company's responsibility. What separate action must the departing manager take?
questions.legal_decision: Notify the Board in writing of the resignation within ten days.
questions.critical_exception: The pharmacist actually resigns as MOR, rather than taking temporary leave; the owner's duties are separate.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacist remains MOR and takes a short temporary absence, this resignation-specific notice does not apply.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy's manager of record resigns on Monday. The owner appoints a qualified replacement and tells the departing pharmacist that all required reporting is the company's responsibility. What separate action must the departing manager take?

choices.text: Notify the Board in writing within ten days of resigning.
choices.why: Correct. The departing MOR has a personal reporting duty even if the owner is arranging a replacement.

choices.text: Notify only the incoming manager and retain the resignation in the pharmacy's records.
choices.why: Incorrect. Internal documentation does not satisfy notice to the Board.

choices.text: Wait for the Board to approve the incoming manager before starting the reporting clock.
choices.why: Incorrect. The notice is tied to the resignation itself.

choices.text: Report the resignation only when the pharmacy permanently closes.
choices.why: Incorrect. Resignation is independently reportable.

choices.text: Use the next biennial personal license renewal to report the change.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule requires written notice on a shorter ten-day timeline.

questions.topic: Work-hour limit across pharmacy assignments
questions.trigger: A technician completes 12 hours of ordinary pharmacy practice at one store and rests for six consecutive hours. The technician is then scheduled at another location of the same chain. There is no extenuating circumstance or urgent patient-care need. Which scheduling decision follows Massachusetts law?
questions.legal_decision: Do not resume pharmacy work until eight consecutive hours of rest have been completed.
questions.critical_exception: The rule addresses the licensee's total practice and rest, not the employer's store-specific payroll; no extenuating circumstance.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If an actual extenuating circumstance requires minimized additional practice in the patient's best interest and is documented, the narrow exception may apply.
questions.stem: A technician completes 12 hours of ordinary pharmacy practice at one store and rests for six consecutive hours. The technician is then scheduled at another location of the same chain. There is no extenuating circumstance or urgent patient-care need. Which scheduling decision follows Massachusetts law?

choices.text: Allow the next shift because each store maintains its own time records.
choices.why: Incorrect. The pharmacy practice limitation is not reset by changing stores.

choices.text: Allow the next shift if the technician handles only Schedule VI prescriptions.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule is not limited to federally controlled drugs.

choices.text: Complete the remaining two hours of consecutive rest before resuming pharmacy practice.
choices.why: Correct. The ordinary limit requires eight consecutive hours of rest before resuming after the stated work period.

choices.text: Allow routine work now if the manager documents ordinary understaffing as a blanket exception.
choices.why: Incorrect. The facts expressly exclude an extenuating circumstance and patient-care necessity.

choices.text: Count a one-hour meal break on the next shift toward the missing consecutive rest.
choices.why: Incorrect. Rest after resuming does not satisfy the prior consecutive-rest requirement.

questions.topic: Annual pharmacy-law CE within a complete renewal cycle
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacist seeking renewal has 20 otherwise eligible contact hours in 2025, including one law hour, and 20 in 2026, including three law hours. Both years meet the live/mediated and daily limits. The pharmacist is not exempt and has no Board-approved exception. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.legal_decision: The general total is met but the 2025 annual law minimum is not; excess 2026 law credit cannot be applied backward.
questions.critical_exception: Calendar-year minimum of two pharmacy-law hours; no carryover or exception.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If 2025 had at least two eligible law hours and all other conditions were satisfied, this law-credit deficiency would be removed.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist seeking renewal has 20 otherwise eligible contact hours in 2025, including one law hour, and 20 in 2026, including three law hours. Both years meet the live/mediated and daily limits. The pharmacist is not exempt and has no Board-approved exception. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.text: The pharmacist meets all CE requirements because the cycle contains four law hours.
choices.why: Incorrect. Law credits must satisfy each year's separate minimum.

choices.text: The pharmacist can apply the extra 2026 law hour to 2025.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule does not permit cross-year carryover.

choices.text: Only the 2026 CE hours matter because the renewal occurs in 2026.
choices.why: Incorrect. The general minimum and law requirement apply in both calendar years.

choices.text: The pharmacist may certify completion if the CE provider accredited both law courses.
choices.why: Incorrect. Provider accreditation does not cure the annual distribution deficiency.

choices.text: The 2025 law requirement is unmet despite the 40-hour total.
choices.why: Correct. One law hour in 2025 is below the two-hour calendar-year requirement.

questions.topic: Technician license by equivalent out-of-state credential
questions.trigger: A technician who meets the Massachusetts age, education and character conditions holds a current license in another state. That state's licensure requirements are substantially equivalent to Massachusetts requirements, and the license is in good standing. Which statement about the Massachusetts initial license application is accurate?
questions.legal_decision: The equivalent good-standing license is an alternative eligibility route; a Massachusetts license still must be issued before practice.
questions.critical_exception: All other Massachusetts application conditions are assumed met, and the out-of-state requirements are substantially equivalent.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the other state's licensure requirements are not substantially equivalent, this route is unavailable and another qualifying pathway is necessary.
questions.stem: A technician who meets the Massachusetts age, education and character conditions holds a current license in another state. That state's licensure requirements are substantially equivalent to Massachusetts requirements, and the license is in good standing. Which statement about the Massachusetts initial license application is accurate?

choices.text: The applicant must obtain national certification despite qualifying through equivalent licensure.
choices.why: Incorrect. National certification is one alternative, not an additional condition of this route.

choices.text: The equivalent license can satisfy the alternative eligibility route, subject to Massachusetts issuance.
choices.why: Correct. Section 8.02 recognizes equivalent good-standing out-of-state licensure.

choices.text: The applicant may start technician work immediately using the other state's license.
choices.why: Incorrect. Massachusetts requires a valid Board-issued technician license.

choices.text: The applicant must first complete 500 trainee hours even under this route.
choices.why: Incorrect. The trainee-hours pathway is a different eligibility option.

choices.text: The employer may issue a temporary state license after checking the credential.
choices.why: Incorrect. The employer is not the Massachusetts licensing authority.

questions.topic: Pending criminal charge without arrest
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts-licensed intern receives formal notice of a pending criminal charge, but has not been arrested or convicted. The intern believes a Board report can wait until the court resolves the matter. Which action complies with the general reporting regulation?
questions.legal_decision: Report the pending criminal charge within 14 calendar days; reporting does not itself establish guilt or automatic discipline.
questions.critical_exception: Actual pending charge, not merely an unfiled allegation; the intern is an individual Board licensee.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If there is merely an allegation and no arrest, pending criminal charge or conviction, the stated criminal-report trigger is absent.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts-licensed intern receives formal notice of a pending criminal charge, but has not been arrested or convicted. The intern believes a Board report can wait until the court resolves the matter. Which action complies with the general reporting regulation?

choices.text: Wait until a conviction occurs because pending matters are confidential.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule expressly includes pending charges.

choices.text: Report only if the criminal charge involves a controlled substance.
choices.why: Incorrect. The reporting clause is not limited to drug-related charges.

choices.text: Have the employer report at the next facility renewal instead of filing personally.
choices.why: Incorrect. The reporting responsibility applies to the individual licensee.

choices.text: Report the pending charge to the Board within 14 calendar days.
choices.why: Correct. A pending charge is an independent reporting trigger.

choices.text: Immediately surrender the intern license without reporting.
choices.why: Incorrect. No automatic surrender follows from the reporting obligation.

questions.topic: Schedule identification: ketamine and carisoprodol
questions.trigger: Which pair correctly identifies the federal and Massachusetts schedules for ketamine and carisoprodol, respectively?
questions.legal_decision: Classify ketamine as Schedule III and carisoprodol as Schedule IV; Massachusetts incorporates the federal schedule lists.
questions.critical_exception: Both are the ordinary drugs, not exempt products.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the selected product is a prescription drug absent from Schedules I–V, Massachusetts generally treats it as Schedule VI.
questions.stem: Which pair correctly identifies the federal and Massachusetts schedules for ketamine and carisoprodol, respectively?

choices.text: Schedule II and Schedule IV.
choices.why: Incorrect. Ketamine is Schedule III, not II.

choices.text: Schedule III and Schedule VI.
choices.why: Incorrect. Carisoprodol is federally Schedule IV.

choices.text: Schedule III and Schedule IV.
choices.why: Correct. Both listings are incorporated into the corresponding Massachusetts schedules.

choices.text: Schedule IV and Schedule III.
choices.why: Incorrect. The two classifications are reversed.

choices.text: Schedule V and Schedule IV.
choices.why: Incorrect. Ketamine is not Schedule V.

questions.topic: Buprenorphine indication and single-fill quantity
questions.trigger: Two otherwise valid prescriptions request a single 90-day supply of a Schedule III buprenorphine product. Prescription X is for treatment of opioid use disorder. Prescription Y is for chronic pain, not opioid use disorder and not an implantable infusion pump. Assume each particular product and indication is clinically lawful, and no other limit applies. Which statement correctly describes the Massachusetts single-fill quantity rule?
questions.legal_decision: Apply the 90-day exception to X but not Y; the ordinary 30-day cap applies to Schedule II/III opioids outside an exception.
questions.critical_exception: The exception depends on the intended treatment or pump category, not simply the molecule.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If Y is prescribed for opioid use disorder instead and all conditions hold, it also falls within the specified 90-day category.
questions.stem: Two otherwise valid prescriptions request a single 90-day supply of a Schedule III buprenorphine product. Prescription X is for treatment of opioid use disorder. Prescription Y is for chronic pain, not opioid use disorder and not an implantable infusion pump. Assume each particular product and indication is clinically lawful, and no other limit applies. Which statement correctly describes the Massachusetts single-fill quantity rule?

choices.text: Both qualify for a 90-day single fill because the active ingredient is buprenorphine.
choices.why: Incorrect. The OUD-treatment exception does not extend automatically to pain treatment.

choices.text: X may qualify for 90 days; Y is subject to the usual 30-day single-fill limit.
choices.why: Correct. The stated indications produce different outcomes under §23(d).

choices.text: Neither qualifies because all Schedule III medications are capped at 30 days.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statute creates specific exceptions including OUD treatment.

choices.text: Y may qualify for 90 days because treatment of chronic pain is long-term.
choices.why: Incorrect. Chronic pain alone is not an enumerated exception to this quantity rule.

choices.text: Both qualify if the patient agrees not to request another prescription for 90 days.
choices.why: Incorrect. Patient agreement does not enlarge the statutory limit.

questions.topic: Out-of-state Schedule II narcotic delivery outside bordering states
questions.trigger: A physician licensed and DEA-registered only in Florida issues an otherwise valid Schedule II narcotic prescription for a Florida resident. The patient visits a Massachusetts retail pharmacy and requests immediate in-person pickup. No Massachusetts prescriber authorization, §18A exception, or qualifying interstate delivery arrangement applies. Which conclusion follows?
questions.legal_decision: Do not use the out-of-state narcotic exception for the in-person pickup; the separate remote interstate pathway requires its specified delivery conditions.
questions.critical_exception: Florida is neither Maine nor contiguous with Massachusetts; the special interstate delivery conditions are absent.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the order instead comes from an appropriately authorized Maine or contiguous-state practitioner within the statutory time and verification conditions, the ordinary out-of-state Schedule II narcotic pathway may apply.
questions.stem: A physician licensed and DEA-registered only in Florida issues an otherwise valid Schedule II narcotic prescription for a Florida resident. The patient visits a Massachusetts retail pharmacy and requests immediate in-person pickup. No Massachusetts prescriber authorization, §18A exception, or qualifying interstate delivery arrangement applies. Which conclusion follows?

choices.text: Fill the prescription because a DEA registration authorizes any in-person interstate dispensing.
choices.why: Incorrect. Massachusetts imposes additional restrictions on this out-of-state Schedule II narcotic order.

choices.text: Fill it if the Florida prescription is less than five days old.
choices.why: Incorrect. Timeliness does not establish the required geographic or special interstate delivery conditions.

choices.text: Fill it after calling the physician because verification removes every interstate restriction.
choices.why: Incorrect. Verification is necessary in applicable pathways but does not create a missing pathway.

choices.text: Fill it only if the patient pays without using insurance.
choices.why: Incorrect. Payment method is irrelevant to the statutory exception.

choices.text: Decline this in-person fill under the stated facts and arrange an appropriate lawful prescription or delivery pathway.
choices.why: Correct. The ordinary geographic route and the separate qualifying interstate delivery route are not satisfied.

critical_error_options.reason: Would dispense a controlled prescription outside the applicable state authorization.

questions.topic: Pharmacist-origin prescription and NPI
questions.trigger: A qualified pharmacist at a Massachusetts community pharmacy is preparing to independently prescribe an eligible oral contraceptive under the August 2026 DPH circular. Prescribing and dispensing will take place at the same licensed location. The pharmacist has no National Provider Identifier, and the patient has completed the appropriate screening. Which statement is correct?
questions.legal_decision: The same-site personal MCSR exception does not waive the pharmacist NPI requirement.
questions.critical_exception: The pharmacist is prescribing under §19F, not merely filling another prescriber's prescription; all other prerequisites are assumed.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacist has the required NPI and all other conditions are met, absence of a separate personal MCSR at the single location does not itself bar the prescribing.
questions.stem: A qualified pharmacist at a Massachusetts community pharmacy is preparing to independently prescribe an eligible oral contraceptive under the August 2026 DPH circular. Prescribing and dispensing will take place at the same licensed location. The pharmacist has no National Provider Identifier, and the patient has completed the appropriate screening. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Obtain an individual DEA number because all Massachusetts prescriptions are federally controlled.
choices.why: Incorrect. The authorized nonfederally scheduled product does not require a DEA number on that basis.

choices.text: Proceed because same-site prescribing and dispensing waive every prescriber identifier.
choices.why: Incorrect. The same-site MCSR exception does not waive the NPI requirement.

choices.text: Use the pharmacy's identifier instead of obtaining the pharmacist's own required NPI.
choices.why: Incorrect. The circular assigns the NPI requirement to the prescribing pharmacist.

choices.text: Obtain the pharmacist's NPI before independently prescribing under this pathway.
choices.why: Correct. The 2026 circular expressly requires the pharmacist to obtain an NPI.

choices.text: Require a physician to sign every pharmacist-origin prescription even after all prerequisites are met.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statute authorizes qualifying pharmacists to prescribe within the specified scope.

questions.citation: M.G.L. c.94C §19F; DCP 26-08-125 General Prescribing Requirements (b)

questions.topic: Additional Schedule IV oral refill quantity exceeds initial quantity
questions.trigger: A patient has a Schedule IV prescription initially filled for 30 tablets, with two refills authorized. The original prescriber calls two months after issuance and requests one additional refill of 60 tablets on the original prescription. The requested refill count would remain within five. Which response is appropriate under the federal additional-refill rule?
questions.legal_decision: Require a new prescription for the proposed 60-tablet refill rather than using the oral additional-refill authorization on the original prescription.
questions.critical_exception: Additional oral refill authorization for Schedule III/IV; quantity of each additional refill cannot exceed the initial fill's authorized quantity.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the additional refill were for 30 tablets and met all count, validity and documentation requirements, the original prescriber could authorize it under the stated rule.
questions.stem: A patient has a Schedule IV prescription initially filled for 30 tablets, with two refills authorized. The original prescriber calls two months after issuance and requests one additional refill of 60 tablets on the original prescription. The requested refill count would remain within five. Which response is appropriate under the federal additional-refill rule?

choices.text: Obtain a new prescription for the proposed larger quantity.
choices.why: Correct. The additional-refill allowance does not permit an additional refill larger than the initial authorized quantity.

choices.text: Accept the 60-tablet oral refill because fewer than five refills have been authorized.
choices.why: Incorrect. The numerical refill limit is only one condition.

choices.text: Record the 60 tablets as a single additional refill because the original prescriber called.
choices.why: Incorrect. The original prescriber's identity does not remove the quantity condition.

choices.text: Treat the additional refill as an extension of the six-month validity period.
choices.why: Incorrect. The original issue date controls validity.

choices.text: Accept the requested quantity because state Schedule VI rules permit some larger supplies.
choices.why: Incorrect. This is a federally Schedule IV prescription.

questions.topic: Nonroutine travel vaccines in nonretail CDTM setting
questions.trigger: A pharmacist in a hospital ambulatory clinic has a compliant CDTM agreement expressly authorizing an indicated nonroutine travel vaccine. A community retail pharmacist has the same immunization training and a community CDTM agreement. Both intend to administer under the special nonroutine-vaccine CDTM provision of Policy 2023-02. Which conclusion is appropriate?
questions.legal_decision: The hospital/clinic CDTM pharmacist may administer if all requirements are met; the special CDTM provision excludes community/retail settings.
questions.critical_exception: The vaccine is nonroutine and the authorization asserted is specifically Policy 2023-02 §I(C), not another independently authorized route.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the community pharmacist is administering a routine vaccine covered under the general policy instead, the community exclusion from §I(C) is not the controlling rule.
questions.stem: A pharmacist in a hospital ambulatory clinic has a compliant CDTM agreement expressly authorizing an indicated nonroutine travel vaccine. A community retail pharmacist has the same immunization training and a community CDTM agreement. Both intend to administer under the special nonroutine-vaccine CDTM provision of Policy 2023-02. Which conclusion is appropriate?

choices.text: Both pharmacists are authorized under the special provision merely because they have CDTM agreements.
choices.why: Incorrect. The nonroutine-vaccine provision specifically excludes community or retail settings.

choices.text: Neither is authorized under the special provision because all travel vaccines require physician administration.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy expressly permits qualifying CDTM pharmacists in eligible settings.

choices.text: Only the community pharmacist qualifies because retail immunization services are the default setting.
choices.why: Incorrect. The special CDTM provision excludes that setting.

choices.text: The clinic pharmacist may qualify if the agreement and all applicable training and other requirements are satisfied.
choices.why: Correct. The nonretail CDTM setting with agreement authorization fits the specified pathway.

choices.text: Either pharmacist can rely on the provision even when the vaccine is not included in the agreement.
choices.why: Incorrect. Inclusion of the vaccine in the CDTM agreement is required.

questions.topic: Pharmacist vaccine administration under Commissioner recommendation
questions.trigger: An adult is eligible under the current Massachusetts DPH Commissioner's routine-vaccine recommendation. That recommendation expressly differs from the manufacturer's original approved usage schedule. Assuming a valid order and all other requirements are met, which authority may the qualified pharmacist follow?
questions.legal_decision: Follow the current applicable DPH Commissioner recommendation under the vaccine policy.
questions.critical_exception: An actual DPH Commissioner recommendation covers the stated population or schedule; not the pharmacist's unsupported decision to depart from approved labeling.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If no applicable Commissioner recommendation or other authorization exists, this specific exception does not support use outside the authorized schedule.
questions.stem: An adult is eligible under the current Massachusetts DPH Commissioner's routine-vaccine recommendation. That recommendation expressly differs from the manufacturer's original approved usage schedule. Assuming a valid order and all other requirements are met, which authority may the qualified pharmacist follow?

choices.text: Only the original manufacturer's schedule, even when DPH has expressly authorized a different schedule.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy specifically permits use under current Commissioner recommendations.

choices.text: Any schedule recommended by the patient's family.
choices.why: Incorrect. Family preference does not confer regulatory authorization.

choices.text: The current applicable DPH Commissioner recommendation.
choices.why: Correct. The vaccine policy permits the specified departure from original approved or authorized product information.

choices.text: Any schedule selected by the pharmacist independently of DPH or other authority.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy does not give unlimited discretion to depart from authorized recommendations.

choices.text: Only a schedule approved by the pharmacy's insurer.
choices.why: Incorrect. Insurance approval does not determine this administration authority.

questions.topic: Counseling of established therapy with significant new directions
questions.trigger: A patient returns for a familiar medication. The authorized directions have changed substantially, and the pharmacist judges the change significant to patient safety. The patient accepts counseling. A trained cashier has already extended the offer to counsel. What is required?
questions.legal_decision: Provide counseling through a pharmacist or pharmacy intern; prior therapy familiarity and a valid offer do not replace counseling when the change is significant.
questions.critical_exception: The pharmacist has judged the changed therapy significant and the patient has not refused.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If this were an unchanged, nonsignificant refill and the patient declined the offer, the actual counseling duty would be assessed under the refusal and offer rules.
questions.stem: A patient returns for a familiar medication. The authorized directions have changed substantially, and the pharmacist judges the change significant to patient safety. The patient accepts counseling. A trained cashier has already extended the offer to counsel. What is required?

choices.text: Allow the cashier to explain the clinical change because the patient already accepted counseling.
choices.why: Incorrect. Extending the offer does not authorize clinical counseling.

choices.text: Provide counseling by the pharmacist or a pharmacy intern under applicable supervision.
choices.why: Correct. A significant therapy change triggers the counseling requirement, and these are the authorized counselors.

choices.text: Rely on the written label alone because the drug is familiar to the patient.
choices.why: Incorrect. The significant change and accepted offer call for actual counseling.

choices.text: Defer counseling until the next unchanged refill because this is not a new drug.
choices.why: Incorrect. A significant change is independently within the rule.

choices.text: Have an ordinary technician interpret the new directions without pharmacist involvement.
choices.why: Incorrect. Technicians cannot provide patient counseling.

critical_error_options.reason: Substitutes unlicensed counseling for the required professional counseling.
Delegates patient counseling to an unauthorized technician.

questions.topic: MassHealth nursing facility dose adjustment and reuse for same resident
questions.trigger: A MassHealth nursing-facility resident has unused, intact unit-dose packages of a medication covered by the return program. The prescriber changes the dose, but the existing supply can safely and lawfully be used to provide the new dose to the same resident. Which actions follow the nursing-facility dosage-change rule? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Use the remaining supply for the resident instead of returning it, document the change, and apply a change-of-directions sticker.
questions.critical_exception: Same resident and existing dosage form can accommodate the newly authorized dosage.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the medication is instead discontinued and meets returnability criteria with no exclusion, the return-for-credit pathway may be required.
questions.stem: A MassHealth nursing-facility resident has unused, intact unit-dose packages of a medication covered by the return program. The prescriber changes the dose, but the existing supply can safely and lawfully be used to provide the new dose to the same resident. Which actions follow the nursing-facility dosage-change rule? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Use the appropriate existing supplies for this same resident instead of returning them solely for the dose change.
choices.why: Correct. The dosage-change rule prioritizes use of the existing compatible supply.

choices.text: Automatically return every unused package for credit regardless of whether it can provide the new dose.
choices.why: Incorrect. The dosage-change exception specifically requires using existing compatible supplies.

choices.text: Document the new dosage in the resident's record.
choices.why: Correct. The facility must record the change.

choices.text: Apply the change-of-directions sticker over the existing directions.
choices.why: Correct. This is one of the expressly specified steps.

choices.text: Use the same packages for a different resident merely because the packaging remains intact.
choices.why: Incorrect. The special rule concerns use for the member whose dosage was changed.

questions.topic: HIPAA insurer request and minimum necessary
questions.trigger: A health plan requests a covered pharmacy's patient's entire five-year prescription record to adjudicate a single routine claim. The pharmacist determines that a much smaller set of records is sufficient for the payment purpose. No authorization or other exception to minimum necessary applies. Which response complies with HIPAA?
questions.legal_decision: Limit the permissible payment disclosure to the minimum necessary; payment generally does not share the treatment exception.
questions.critical_exception: Routine payment disclosure, not a request by a provider for treatment or a required-by-law disclosure.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a health care provider requests the information for treatment, the HIPAA minimum-necessary rule does not apply to that treatment disclosure, although other applicable law may.
questions.stem: A health plan requests a covered pharmacy's patient's entire five-year prescription record to adjudicate a single routine claim. The pharmacist determines that a much smaller set of records is sufficient for the payment purpose. No authorization or other exception to minimum necessary applies. Which response complies with HIPAA?

choices.text: Release the entire record because the plan has requested it for payment.
choices.why: Incorrect. The minimum-necessary standard applies to the stated payment disclosure.

choices.text: Refuse any claim-related disclosure unless the patient signs a separate authorization.
choices.why: Incorrect. HIPAA generally permits appropriate payment disclosures without separate authorization.

choices.text: Treat the plan as a treatment provider solely because it finances health care.
choices.why: Incorrect. The purpose of this request is claim payment.

choices.text: Release only the information reasonably necessary for the identified claim.
choices.why: Correct. The permitted payment disclosure must be appropriately limited under the stated facts.

choices.text: Send the entire record and instruct the plan to delete unrelated information afterward.
choices.why: Incorrect. The pharmacy must apply the disclosure limitation before releasing PHI.

questions.topic: Earliest fill date within otherwise valid Schedule II period
questions.trigger: An otherwise lawful Massachusetts Schedule II prescription is one of multiple prescriptions issued November 1 under the federal multiple-prescription provision. It states that it cannot be filled before November 21. On November 18 the patient's insurer will pay and the prescriber has not issued a replacement. What may the pharmacist do?
questions.legal_decision: Do not fill before the prescribed earliest date; verify state validity when dispensing becomes eligible.
questions.critical_exception: The earliest-fill instruction is part of the qualifying prescription and has not been superseded; the original is otherwise still within its Massachusetts 30-day period.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If presented November 21 and all other requirements are satisfied, the earliest-fill restriction no longer bars dispensing.
questions.stem: An otherwise lawful Massachusetts Schedule II prescription is one of multiple prescriptions issued November 1 under the federal multiple-prescription provision. It states that it cannot be filled before November 21. On November 18 the patient's insurer will pay and the prescriber has not issued a replacement. What may the pharmacist do?

choices.text: Fill on November 18 because the prescription has not yet expired.
choices.why: Incorrect. Being within the validity period does not override the earliest-fill restriction.

choices.text: Fill on November 18 because the insurance system accepted the claim.
choices.why: Incorrect. Payer acceptance does not override the practitioner's legally effective date.

choices.text: Wait until the specified earliest-fill date and reassess validity and safety.
choices.why: Correct. The federal rule prohibits filling before that date.

choices.text: Wait 30 days after November 21 because the earliest-fill date restarts validity.
choices.why: Incorrect. State validity is measured from issuance, not the earliest-fill date.

choices.text: Convert the prescription to a refill on the previous Schedule II order.
choices.why: Incorrect. Schedule II refills are prohibited.

critical_error_options.reason: Dispenses before a legally binding earliest-fill date.

questions.topic: Computer-printed controlled prescription with no manual signature
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts practitioner experiences a qualifying electronic-prescribing failure. The practitioner prints a computer-generated paper Schedule IV prescription with a typed prescriber name but no manual signature. The patient presents it as a written prescription. It is not a lawfully communicated oral order. What should the pharmacist do?
questions.legal_decision: Do not dispense on this unsigned written prescription; obtain a properly signed written order or another lawful prescription.
questions.critical_exception: The electronic-prescribing exception permits a written route but does not make a typed name a valid handwritten signature on a printed controlled prescription.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the practitioner manually signs the otherwise valid printed prescription and the exception applies, this signature defect is resolved.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts practitioner experiences a qualifying electronic-prescribing failure. The practitioner prints a computer-generated paper Schedule IV prescription with a typed prescriber name but no manual signature. The patient presents it as a written prescription. It is not a lawfully communicated oral order. What should the pharmacist do?

choices.text: Obtain a properly signed written prescription or a different lawful order before dispensing.
choices.why: Correct. A computer-generated printed controlled prescription must be manually signed.

choices.text: Accept the typed prescriber name as an electronic signature even though the order was printed.
choices.why: Incorrect. An electronic signature under Part 1311 is not the same as a typed name on paper.

choices.text: Accept the unsigned order because the outage qualifies as an exception to ePrescribing.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exception changes transmission options, not the signature requirement.

choices.text: Have the patient sign on behalf of the practitioner.
choices.why: Incorrect. The patient's signature cannot substitute for practitioner issuance.

choices.text: Treat the printed document as a valid oral prescription without any oral authorization.
choices.why: Incorrect. No valid oral order was communicated in the stated facts.

critical_error_options.reason: Dispenses an unsigned controlled paper order.
Treats the transmission exception as a waiver of prescription validity.

questions.topic: Sending pharmacist documentation after manual controlled refill transfer
questions.trigger: At a patient's request, a pharmacist completes a lawful one-time manual transfer of the remaining refills on a paper Schedule IV prescription to an unrelated pharmacy. Which entries must the transferring pharmacist make on the original record? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Invalidate the paper original and document receiving pharmacy and pharmacist identifiers plus transfer date and transferring pharmacist.
questions.critical_exception: Manual refill transfer of an existing paper prescription; not an electronic initial-fill transfer.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the order is being transferred electronically, the corresponding transfer information must be added to the electronic prescription record rather than marking the paper original.
questions.stem: At a patient's request, a pharmacist completes a lawful one-time manual transfer of the remaining refills on a paper Schedule IV prescription to an unrelated pharmacy. Which entries must the transferring pharmacist make on the original record? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Mark the original prescription void.
choices.why: Correct. The sending pharmacist must invalidate the original paper prescription.

choices.text: Keep the original active so both pharmacies can refill it independently.
choices.why: Incorrect. The transfer must not leave duplicative refill authority at both stores.

choices.text: Record the receiving pharmacy's name, address, DEA number and the receiving pharmacist's name.
choices.why: Correct. These destination identifiers are required.

choices.text: Document only the number of refills remaining and destroy the original.
choices.why: Incorrect. The original transfer record must be retained with required annotations.

choices.text: Record the transfer date and the name of the transferring pharmacist.
choices.why: Correct. The regulation expressly requires both entries.

critical_error_options.reason: Leaves duplicate active dispensing authority after a completed transfer.
Destroys a required controlled prescription record.

questions.topic: DUR identifies therapeutic duplication after new order
questions.trigger: A patient's profile shows an active lisinopril prescription. A new prescription for enalapril arrives from a different prescriber, with no instruction to stop the first medication. The patient confirms taking lisinopril. No explanation for concurrent use is available. Which actions follow Massachusetts prospective DUR duties? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Identify the possible therapeutic duplication, obtain appropriate clarification before release, and document the intervention.
questions.critical_exception: New prescription with unresolved clinically significant duplication; no established plan to replace the first medication.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If clarification establishes that enalapril is intended to replace lisinopril and the regimen is appropriate, the pharmacist may proceed after reconciliation and other checks.
questions.stem: A patient's profile shows an active lisinopril prescription. A new prescription for enalapril arrives from a different prescriber, with no instruction to stop the first medication. The patient confirms taking lisinopril. No explanation for concurrent use is available. Which actions follow Massachusetts prospective DUR duties? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Assess the possible therapeutic duplication and clarify the intended regimen.
choices.why: Correct. Prospective DUR expressly includes therapeutic duplication.

choices.text: Dispense both because each prescriber separately authorized a drug.
choices.why: Incorrect. Separate prescriber authorization does not resolve duplication.

choices.text: Let a technician independently determine whether both ACE inhibitors should be used.
choices.why: Incorrect. This clinical judgment belongs to the pharmacist.

choices.text: Document the pharmacist's response to the DUR finding.
choices.why: Correct. Actions taken in response to a DUR must be documented.

choices.text: Delete the first medication from the profile without confirming its status.
choices.why: Incorrect. An unsupported deletion does not establish a safe regimen.

critical_error_options.reason: Releases an unresolved clinically significant therapeutic duplication.

questions.topic: Schedule VI continuity dispensing and smallest unit-of-use
questions.trigger: A stable patient's otherwise appropriate Schedule VI maintenance medication is supplied only in a sealed, manufacturer unit-of-use package providing 28 days of treatment. It is the smallest available unit-of-use package. The prescription has no refills, and despite timely attempts the pharmacist cannot obtain authorization. The pharmacist judges continuity appropriate and all other legal conditions are met. Which dispensing quantity is permitted?
questions.legal_decision: May provide the smallest available unit-of-use package even when it exceeds 14 days, under the narrow Schedule VI continuity rule.
questions.critical_exception: The prescription is Schedule VI; prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in time; the 28-day package is truly the smallest available unit-of-use.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a suitable smaller unit-of-use package containing 14 days or less is available, that fact removes the stated basis for choosing the 28-day package.
questions.stem: A stable patient's otherwise appropriate Schedule VI maintenance medication is supplied only in a sealed, manufacturer unit-of-use package providing 28 days of treatment. It is the smallest available unit-of-use package. The prescription has no refills, and despite timely attempts the pharmacist cannot obtain authorization. The pharmacist judges continuity appropriate and all other legal conditions are met. Which dispensing quantity is permitted?

choices.text: No supply may be provided because the ordinary authorized refills are exhausted.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation supplies a narrow continuity pathway when authorization cannot be obtained in time.

choices.text: Provide any quantity the patient requests, including six months.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exception has an express quantity limitation.

choices.text: Provide exactly 14 days by opening every manufacturer unit-of-use package.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule alternatively permits the smallest available unit-of-use packaging.

choices.text: Provide the 28-day smallest available unit-of-use package using professional judgment.
choices.why: Correct. The alternative unit-of-use limitation is satisfied under the stated facts.

choices.text: Create unlimited refills on the original prescription because the patient is stable.
choices.why: Incorrect. The continuity supply does not confer ongoing refill authorization.

questions.topic: Tablet count required on Massachusetts prescription container
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts community pharmacy dispenses 90 tablets of an ordinary Schedule VI prescription medicine. Its patient-specific container label contains the other statutory elements but omits the actual number of tablets in the container. Which action is required?
questions.legal_decision: Include the number of tablets in the dispensed container label under Massachusetts law.
questions.critical_exception: The drug is dispensed as tablets; no special labeling exception applies.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the medication is dispensed in a non-tablet/non-capsule dosage form, the specific tablet/capsule count clause is not triggered.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy dispenses 90 tablets of an ordinary Schedule VI prescription medicine. Its patient-specific container label contains the other statutory elements but omits the actual number of tablets in the container. Which action is required?

choices.text: Add the actual tablet count to the patient-specific container label.
choices.why: Correct. Massachusetts expressly requires the count for tablets or capsules.

choices.text: Record the quantity only in the computer and leave the container label unchanged.
choices.why: Incorrect. An internal record is not the required container-label statement.

choices.text: Add the count only if the medicine is federally Schedule II.
choices.why: Incorrect. The state controlled-substance labeling statute includes Schedule VI drugs.

choices.text: Replace directions for use with the quantity on the label.
choices.why: Incorrect. Both ordinary directions and the tablet count remain required.

choices.text: Add the quantity only if the patient requests large-print directions.
choices.why: Incorrect. The quantity requirement is independent of the accessibility provision.

questions.topic: Pseudoephedrine locked cabinet in customer area
questions.trigger: A pharmacy displays pseudoephedrine products in a locked glass cabinet on the sales floor. Staff control the key, customers cannot access the products before sale, and staff hand the product directly to the buyer after completing all applicable sale requirements. Which conclusion follows the federal placement rule?
questions.legal_decision: The locked sales-floor cabinet can qualify as behind-the-counter placement when direct access is prevented and the product is handed to the buyer.
questions.critical_exception: All separate quantity, ID, logbook, certification and applicable state duties are assumed met.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If customers can open the cabinet and remove the product before the sale, the stated placement condition is not satisfied.
questions.stem: A pharmacy displays pseudoephedrine products in a locked glass cabinet on the sales floor. Staff control the key, customers cannot access the products before sale, and staff hand the product directly to the buyer after completing all applicable sale requirements. Which conclusion follows the federal placement rule?

choices.text: The arrangement is prohibited unless the cabinet is physically behind the prescription counter.
choices.why: Incorrect. A locked cabinet in a customer-accessible area can meet the placement standard.

choices.text: The cabinet location is permissible under the described access and handoff controls.
choices.why: Correct. The rule treats locked, customer-inaccessible storage as behind-the-counter placement.

choices.text: Allow customers to remove the product before paying if a staff member observes them.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule requires prevention of direct access before sale.

choices.text: Leave the product on an open shelf because the purchaser has acceptable identification.
choices.why: Incorrect. Identification does not replace the placement requirement.

choices.text: Allow the purchaser to retrieve the product independently from the unlocked cabinet after registration.
choices.why: Incorrect. The seller must deliver the product directly into purchaser custody.

questions.topic: DSCSA specific patient need versus replenishing stock
questions.trigger: Pharmacy A has a prescription for an identified patient but lacks the covered prescription drug. It buys the necessary package from unrelated Pharmacy B for this prescription. Pharmacy A later proposes buying an additional case to replenish general inventory. Both pharmacies are properly authorized, and no other exemption applies. Which statement correctly describes the DSCSA product-tracing exception?
questions.legal_decision: Apply the specific-patient-need tracing exception to the first transaction, not the general inventory purchase.
questions.critical_exception: Only the first sale fills an identified patient's prescription; general stock replenishment is outside the statutory definition.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the second transfer is instead solely to fill another identified patient's prescription, the specific-patient-need tracing exception may apply to it as well.
questions.stem: Pharmacy A has a prescription for an identified patient but lacks the covered prescription drug. It buys the necessary package from unrelated Pharmacy B for this prescription. Pharmacy A later proposes buying an additional case to replenish general inventory. Both pharmacies are properly authorized, and no other exemption applies. Which statement correctly describes the DSCSA product-tracing exception?

choices.text: Both sales qualify because pharmacies may transfer prescription drugs to one another.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exception does not cover general replenishment.

choices.text: Neither sale qualifies because the pharmacies are unrelated.
choices.why: Incorrect. The identified-patient exception does not depend on common ownership.

choices.text: The first sale qualifies; the general replenishment sale does not qualify under this exception.
choices.why: Correct. A specific patient need means filling an identified patient's prescription, not acquiring anticipated stock.

choices.text: The second sale qualifies if the purchaser expects demand later that week.
choices.why: Incorrect. Expected demand is expressly distinguished from the specific-patient need.

choices.text: The first sale eliminates all other applicable supply-chain and pharmacy duties.
choices.why: Incorrect. This is a product-tracing exception, not a blanket regulatory exemption.

questions.citation: 21 USC 360eee(19), 360eee-1(d)(1)(A)(ii); FDA DSCSA product tracing FAQ

questions.topic: Biennial inventory for separate registered retail locations
questions.trigger: A chain owns two pharmacies, each separately DEA-registered. On the same date both pharmacies count all federally controlled stock. Management proposes preparing only one combined inventory document listing the total quantities across both stores without separate location counts. Which action complies with federal inventory requirements?
questions.legal_decision: Maintain a complete separate inventory for each registered location rather than only a consolidated total.
questions.critical_exception: Two separately registered dispensing locations; no applicable special inventory exception.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the stock is all under one registered location's control, it is included in that location's inventory under the applicable on-hand rule.
questions.stem: A chain owns two pharmacies, each separately DEA-registered. On the same date both pharmacies count all federally controlled stock. Management proposes preparing only one combined inventory document listing the total quantities across both stores without separate location counts. Which action complies with federal inventory requirements?

choices.text: Keep the combined inventory only, because the stores have common ownership.
choices.why: Incorrect. Common ownership does not eliminate separate registered-location inventories.

choices.text: Maintain a separate inventory for each location.
choices.why: Correct. The federal rule expressly requires separate inventories for each registered location.

choices.text: Record only Schedule II stock separately; pool all Schedule III–V stock.
choices.why: Incorrect. The location requirement applies to federally controlled inventories, not just Schedule II.

choices.text: Count one store this year and the other after four years to avoid duplicate records.
choices.why: Incorrect. Each registrant must satisfy the biennial requirement.

choices.text: Combine the stores as long as their counts were taken on the same calendar day.
choices.why: Incorrect. The shared inventory date does not satisfy location-specific accountability.

questions.topic: USP immediate-use single-dose vial cannot be shared across patients
questions.trigger: In a patient-care area, a qualified clinician prepares an immediate-use CSP for Patient A using a single-dose vial. The vial has unused drug after the preparation is complete. A second patient has an order for the same drug, and both preparations would be administered immediately. Which action follows the USP immediate-use provision?
questions.legal_decision: Discard the unused portion of the single-dose starting component once Patient A's preparation is complete; use a separate appropriate container for Patient B.
questions.critical_exception: The scenario is the immediate-use CSP provision, not the distinct rules for eligible single-dose containers used within classified pharmacy compounding areas.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the container were an appropriate multiple-dose product, the single-dose-specific one-patient rule would not itself decide the case, though other requirements remain.
questions.stem: In a patient-care area, a qualified clinician prepares an immediate-use CSP for Patient A using a single-dose vial. The vial has unused drug after the preparation is complete. A second patient has an order for the same drug, and both preparations would be administered immediately. Which action follows the USP immediate-use provision?

choices.text: Discard the unused portion and use a suitable separate container for the second patient's preparation.
choices.why: Correct. The immediate-use provision does not permit sharing a single-dose container between patients.

choices.text: Use the remainder for the second patient if both preparations are started within four hours.
choices.why: Incorrect. The immediate-use time limit does not remove the one-patient condition.

choices.text: Label the vial with the time of first puncture and reuse it for either patient throughout the shift.
choices.why: Incorrect. A label does not convert a single-dose vial into a shared multi-patient source.

choices.text: Apply the classified-PEC component in-use time without regard to the immediate-use setting.
choices.why: Incorrect. That is a different workflow and does not override the immediate-use condition.

choices.text: Share the vial as long as the same clinician prepares both doses.
choices.why: Incorrect. Staff identity does not create a multi-patient exception.

critical_error_options.reason: Reuses an immediate-use single-dose component for another patient.

questions.topic: 503A bulk API eligibility and certificate of analysis
questions.trigger: A 503A pharmacy has a patient-specific prescription for a nonsterile compound. The proposed bulk active ingredient has an applicable USP/NF monograph and was manufactured by an FDA-registered establishment. The pharmacy cannot obtain a valid certificate of analysis for the supplied material. Which conditions must the pharmacist satisfy before relying on section 503A for this preparation? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Require the applicable monograph and compounding standards, a valid certificate of analysis and a registered manufacturing establishment.
questions.critical_exception: Bulk drug substance used under 503A; valid patient-specific order does not waive ingredient eligibility.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a valid certificate of analysis is obtained and compliance with the applicable standards and registered-manufacturer requirement is established, the specified ingredient deficiency is resolved.
questions.stem: A 503A pharmacy has a patient-specific prescription for a nonsterile compound. The proposed bulk active ingredient has an applicable USP/NF monograph and was manufactured by an FDA-registered establishment. The pharmacy cannot obtain a valid certificate of analysis for the supplied material. Which conditions must the pharmacist satisfy before relying on section 503A for this preparation? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Use the bulk ingredient because the prescriber has identified the patient.
choices.why: Incorrect. A patient-specific prescription does not eliminate the bulk-substance conditions.

choices.text: Confirm compliance with the applicable USP/NF monograph and compounding standards.
choices.why: Correct. The existing monograph controls the applicable ingredient eligibility pathway.

choices.text: Obtain a valid certificate of analysis for the bulk substance.
choices.why: Correct. A valid certificate of analysis is separately required.

choices.text: Confirm that the ingredient was manufactured by an establishment registered with FDA.
choices.why: Correct. The statute requires a registered manufacturing establishment.

choices.text: Use an unsigned sales invoice as the certificate of analysis.
choices.why: Incorrect. An ordinary invoice does not establish the required analytical certification.

questions.citation: 21 USC 353a(b)(1)(A)(i)-(iii); FDA Bulk Drug Substances Used in Compounding Under Section 503A

critical_error_options.reason: Uses bulk material despite unmet federal ingredient eligibility conditions.

questions.topic: Retail pharmacy receipt record for central-filled Schedule II prescription
questions.trigger: A properly authorized central-fill pharmacy returns a prepared Schedule II prescription to its participating Massachusetts retail pharmacy using a contract carrier. All required prescription transmission and labeling information is already correct. Which entries must the retail pharmacy retain for receipt of the filled prescription? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.
questions.legal_decision: Record receipt date, method of delivery and identity of retail pharmacy employee accepting delivery.
questions.critical_exception: Retail receiving role after central fulfillment; not central pharmacy's own filling record.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the retail pharmacy prepares the prescription itself instead, the special receipt-of-central-filled-prescription record requirement is not triggered.
questions.stem: A properly authorized central-fill pharmacy returns a prepared Schedule II prescription to its participating Massachusetts retail pharmacy using a contract carrier. All required prescription transmission and labeling information is already correct. Which entries must the retail pharmacy retain for receipt of the filled prescription? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Record the date the filled prescription was received at retail.
choices.why: Correct. Receipt date is explicitly required.

choices.text: Record only the date the central pharmacy prepared the prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. Preparation date alone does not establish receipt.

choices.text: Record the method of delivery, such as contract carrier.
choices.why: Correct. The receipt record must identify the delivery method.

choices.text: Omit the receiver's identity because the delivery carrier is contracted.
choices.why: Incorrect. The name of the retail employee accepting delivery is independently required.

choices.text: Record the name of the retail pharmacy employee accepting delivery.
choices.why: Correct. The regulation requires this identity.

questions.topic: Board rejects pharmacy plan of correction
questions.trigger: The Board returns a pharmacy's submitted plan of correction as unacceptable because the plan does not meet the applicable requirements. What is the default deadline to submit a revised plan under 247 CMR 9.25(5)?
questions.legal_decision: Submit a revised plan of correction within seven days.
questions.critical_exception: This is a rejected plan, not the initial inspection report or first plan deadline.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacy is submitting the original plan following the deficiency report, the usual initial deadline is 21 days or the timeframe directed by the Board.
questions.stem: The Board returns a pharmacy's submitted plan of correction as unacceptable because the plan does not meet the applicable requirements. What is the default deadline to submit a revised plan under 247 CMR 9.25(5)?

choices.text: Within 14 days, the general inspection-report forwarding period.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rejected-plan deadline is distinct from reporting an outside inspection report.

choices.text: Within 21 days, the ordinary initial plan-of-correction period.
choices.why: Incorrect. The initial-plan rule does not govern a rejected plan's revision.

choices.text: At the next scheduled pharmacy renewal.
choices.why: Incorrect. Renewal timing does not satisfy the revision requirement.

choices.text: Within seven days after the plan is returned as unacceptable.
choices.why: Correct. The regulation expressly states the seven-day revision period.

choices.text: Within 30 days of the original inspection, regardless of rejection date.
choices.why: Incorrect. That is not the applicable revised-plan deadline.
